citeAs: Zewei Ye, Weifeng Lu, Minghao Ye, Tao Lin, Shuo Yang, Junchi Yan, Bo Zhao (2025). RoboFAC: A Comprehensive Framework for Robotic Failure Analysis and Correction. arXiv:2505.12224.
creator: Zewei Ye, Weifeng Lu, Minghao Ye, Tao Lin, Shuo Yang, Junchi Yan, Bo Zhao (Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Harbin Institute of Technology Shenzhen)
description: RoboFAC dataset is a large-scale, failure-centric video question-answering dataset for robotic manipulation, comprising 9,440 erroneous manipulation trajectories and 78,623 QA pairs across 53 scenes in both simulation and real-world environments. It covers 14 simulated tasks and 6 real-world tasks with six systematically categorized failure types spanning three hierarchical levels (task planning, motion planning, and execution control). The dataset includes eight question types covering task understanding, failure analysis, and failure correction, with rich multi-dimensional annotations.
name: RoboFAC dataset
rai:annotationsPerItem: 8 QA pairs per trajectory (one per question type: task identification, task planning, failure detection, failure identification, failure locating, failure explanation, high-level correction, low-level correction). For quality control, 10% of samples received 2 independent human quality ratings.
rai:annotatorDemographics: Annotators were drawn from a shared annotator pool. Each selected sample (10% of dataset) was assigned to two randomly chosen annotators from the pool to avoid systematic pairing bias. No further demographic information is provided.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Human verification was performed on a random 10% sample of the dataset, with each selected sample assigned to two independent annotators from a shared annotator pool. Annotators provided quality ratings on a 0–3 ordinal scale and confidence scores on a 1–3 scale. Inter-annotator agreement was measured using Krippendorff's α with an ordinal distance metric, obtaining α = 0.86, indicating high inter-annotator reliability. After human verification, 8,559 trajectories were retained and 3,809 were removed. The average annotator confidence was 2.6.
rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: Custom annotation pipeline using GPT-4o for automated annotation of failure explanation, high-level correction, and low-level correction question types; human annotators from a shared annotator pool for quality verification.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Raw data was annotated to construct video-based QA samples for eight question types. For five question types (task identification, task planning, failure detection, failure identification, failure locating), reference answers were directly extracted from textual descriptions. For three types (failure explanation, high-level correction, low-level correction), GPT-4o was used with structured prompts including task, subtask, error type, error stage, error detail, correction suggestion, and perturbation information to generate reference answers. Five question templates were provided per question type, with one randomly sampled per QA pair.
rai:dataBiases: To prevent models from overfitting to failure patterns, the dataset also includes successful trajectories (1,282 success trajectories alongside 9,440 failure trajectories). To account for visual diversity and avoid domain-specific biases, variations in background, camera viewpoints, and object configurations were intentionally introduced across 53 scenes.
rai:dataCollection: Simulation data was collected for 14 robotic tasks in the ManiSkill environment, augmented with objects from the YCB Object Dataset and scenes from ReplicaCAD and AI2-THOR. Expert policies were defined by specifying target end-effector poses, and failure data was generated by replacing expert policies with code snippets that produce erroneous trajectories. Real-world data was collected for 6 tasks via teleoperation using the SO-100 robotic arm. Each video was accompanied by a textual description including the substage of failure, failure taxonomy, and detailed error explanation.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw data consists of robotic manipulation videos (failure and success trajectories) from both simulation (ManiSkill environment) and real-world (SO-100 robotic arm via teleoperation), along with corresponding textual descriptions including substage information, failure taxonomy, error details, and perturbed poses. The dataset contains 4,793K frames across 10,722 trajectories (9,440 failure + 1,282 success), spanning 53 scenes.
rai:dataCollectionType: Physical data collection, Software Collection, Experiments
rai:dataLimitations: The current integration of RoboFAC correction suggestions into robotic systems is not yet fully seamless. The framework is currently applied exclusively to end-to-end VLA models, and has not been extended to hierarchical policies where high-level and low-level corrections are applied to the planner and controller respectively.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: A three-stage quality control process was applied: (1) Simulation validation enforcing physical validity constraints including unexpected environment collision detection (robot-object and self-collision checks) and trajectory discontinuity detection by examining joint-level temporal differences; (2) LLM-based annotation validation requiring structured JSON outputs following a predefined schema with automatic parsing and schema validation; (3) Human verification with quality ratings, where samples receiving ratings of 0 or 1 were removed from the final dataset.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset enables systematic failure diagnosis and recovery in robotic manipulation, enhancing VLA robustness in open-world scenarios. By enabling lightweight on-device models to match large proprietary models, it reduces dependency on high-latency cloud APIs, making robust robotic systems more accessible and practical for real-world deployment.
rai:dataUseCases: Training and evaluating multimodal models for robotic failure analysis and correction, including task understanding, failure detection, failure identification, failure locating, failure explanation, and corrective reasoning. The dataset supports development of lightweight models for on-device deployment as external supervisors in VLA robotic control pipelines to enable real-time failure detection and recovery.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: GPT-4o was used to generate reference answers for three question types: failure explanation, high-level correction, and low-level correction. GPT-4 was also used as a scoring agent during evaluation to assess model responses across correctness, relevance, and completeness dimensions.

evidence.name: We construct a large-scale failure-centric dataset comprising 9,440 erroneous manipulation trajectories and 78,623 QA pairs across 53 scenes in both simulation and real-world environments, with systematically categorized failure types.
evidence.description: The RoboFAC dataset encompasses robotic tasks of varying complexity, ranging from simple short-horizon tasks to complex long-horizon tasks, and tasks executed in dynamic environments. It includes 14 simulated tasks and 6 real-world tasks, with two of the real-world tasks not present in the simulation environment. The dataset includes six types of failures, spanning three hierarchical levels of error.

evidence.rai:dataCollectionType: Real-World Data. We collected real-world data for 6 tasks, including two tasks that are not present in the simulation dataset. Data collection is performed via teleoperation using the SO-100 robotic arm. As with the simulation data, each video is accompanied by a corresponding textual description.
evidence.rai:dataCollectionRawData: During data collection, we record each robotic failure video along with a corresponding descriptive text. The description includes the substage where the failure occurred, the taxonomy of failure, and a detailed textual explanation of the error. For failures caused by perturbations in the end-effector pose, we also record the perturbed pose.
evidence.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: For each sample, the reference answer is generated based on the textual description associated with the video. For five question types–task identification, task planning, failure detection, failure identification, and failure locating–the reference answers can be directly extracted from the corresponding textual description, as they have well-defined ground truths. For the remaining three types-failure explanation, high-level correction, and low-level correction-we utilize both the video and its corresponding textual description as inputs to GPT-4o to generate the reference answers.
evidence.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: We randomly sample 10% of the dataset and assign each selected sample to two randomly chosen annotators from the annotator pool. Each annotator provides a quality score on a four-level ordinal scale. To measure global annotation consistency under this sparse multi-rater setting, we compute Krippendorff's α with an ordinal distance metric, obtaining α = 0.86, which indicates high inter-annotator reliability.
evidence.rai:annotationsPerItem: We annotate the raw data to construct video-based QA samples corresponding to eight question types, which are described in detail in Section 4. These eight question types comprehensively evaluate a model's ability in Task Understanding, Failure Analysis, and Failure Correction based on robot manipulation videos. For each question type, we provide five question templates.
evidence.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: For the failure explanation, high-level correction, and low-level correction questions, we employed GPT-4o to annotate the data. Specifically, we constructed prompts using the description files obtained during video collection. We use the prompt paired with the corresponding videos to request GPT-4o.
evidence.rai:machineAnnotationTools: For the failure explanation, high-level correction, and low-level correction questions, we employed GPT-4o to annotate the data. Specifically, we constructed prompts using the description files obtained during video collection. We use the prompt paired with the corresponding videos to request GPT-4o.
evidence.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: To ensure the reliability of the generated dataset, we adopt a three-stage quality control pipeline covering simulation validation, LLM-based annotation verification, and human consistency evaluation. During motion planning, we enforce physical validity constraints to eliminate spurious failures. evidence.rai:dataUseCases: Leveraging the RoboFAC dataset, we build an MLLM (RoboFAC model) capable of robotic task understanding, failure analysis, and corrective reasoning from robot videos. By explicitly training on structured failure analysis and correction data, our approach enables a relatively lightweight open-source model to match–and even surpass–general-purpose large models such as GPT-4o, while supporting low-latency and on-device deployment.
evidence.rai:dataSocialImpact: Experimental results demonstrate that RoboFAC achieves a 34.1% higher failure analysis accuracy compared to GPT-4o. Furthermore, we integrated RoboFAC as an external supervisor in a real-world VLA control pipeline, yielding a 29.1% relative improvement across four tasks while significantly reducing latency relative to GPT-4o. These results demonstrate that RoboFAC enables systematic failure diagnosis and recovery, significantly enhancing VLA recovery capabilities.
evidence.rai:dataLimitations: While RoboFAC's correction suggestions effectively assist VLA models in recovering from failures, the current integration into robotic systems is not yet fully seamless. Future work will explore more natural and automated mechanisms for delivering correction suggestions, which could further enable automated failure recovery data collection. Additionally, our current work applies RoboFAC exclusively to end-to-end VLA models.
evidence.rai:dataBiases: To prevent models from overfitting to failure patterns, we also collect 1,160 successful trajectories from simulation and 122 successful trajectories from real-world executions. Rather than merely collecting diverse scenes, we intentionally vary backgrounds, object configurations, and camera viewpoints to expose the model to realistic visual perturbations, thereby improving its robustness to domain shifts.
evidence.rai:annotatorDemographics: For consistency evaluation, 10% of the samples are randomly selected and assigned to two annotators independently. The remaining 90% of samples are assigned to a single annotator. Annotators are randomly drawn from a shared annotator pool to avoid systematic pairing bias.
